# Tech deep dive {background-color="#1a1a00"}

::: {.notes}
About 8 minutes.
:::

## Behind the curtain: one round

```{=html}
{{< include images/_round_flow.svg >}}
```

::: {.notes}
The browser is the clock: it asks for each round when the last one has played. The director, plain Python, plans the
round; llama.cpp writes it under a grammar; the parser cuts the stream into lines as they arrive, and each line goes to
the voice before the next is written. When the radio listens, the listener's words come back through Whisper.

WHY THE BROWSER IS THE CLOCK — decided 2026-09-21 among three placements: (1) the browser as metronome, the server as
director — adopted; (2) a server-side loop pushing to the page — the upgrade for an unattended booth, nothing in (1)
blocks it; (3) an external process polling — rejected. The reason: each decision sits where its information is — the
story on the server, time in the browser, which alone knows when the audio has finished. It reuses the page's
existing server-sent events, and cost a day less. Its one weakness: the browser tab must stay in the foreground.

THE PAGE'S STATES — idle → generating → playing → listening → idle. Generating: lines stream in and the first ones
already play while the model writes the rest. Listening is entered only when the audio queues are empty: half-duplex
by construction, so the microphone never hears the cast and Whisper gets only the listener.

ONE ROUND, IN NUMBERS (measured on the A6000)
- The gap between rounds: 3.7-4.9 s once warm (6.8 s for a run's first round, the voice cold; 8.4 s after a trim):
  the model's first line takes 0.76-0.94 s through the app and the tunnel, then the voice synthesizes the first chunk.
  The static bed rises in that gap, so it never sounds dead.
- The request: one POST to llama.cpp's /v1/chat/completions, streamed, carrying the whole show so far, the GBNF grammar
  in a top-level "grammar" field, max_tokens 512, and a seed (the run's seed plus the round's number).
- The prompt: the cast sheet as the system message — identical every time, so the server reuses its cache and only
  the new part is read fresh; the system message starts with /no_think, which Nemotron's chat template turns into an
  empty, closed <think></think> — so the reply, and the grammar, start in the script, not in hidden reasoning.
- The grammar is applied at sampling: before each token, every token that would break the format is removed. When the
  model already wants a legal token, nothing changes — same seed, same text: measured cost 0.3-0.5 % per token; about
  10 % when it has to overrule the model.
- The voice: each line is cut into chunks of whole sentences (up to about 100 characters) and each chunk is one
  request to tts-serve, with the speaker's reference clip for the line's mood.
- Server timings measure the work, not the wait: the app keeps the server's own token counts (prompt read fresh,
  reused from cache, written) — they size the script for the trim.

NOT BUILT (a follow-up): prefetching round N+1 while round N plays, which would hide the gap.
:::

## The director, in plain Python {.smaller .director}

```{.python}
def plan_round(run: Run, story: Story, show: ShowConfig, played_s: float = 0.0,
               transcript: Optional[str] = None) -> RoundPlan:
    n = len(run.rounds) + 1
    rng = random.Random(f"{run.seed}:{n}")
    if not run.rounds:
        return _orientation(run, story, show, rng, sign_on=True)
    if run.rounds[-1].kind in LISTENS:
        return _after_listening(run, story, show, (transcript or "").strip(), rng)
    if run.rounds[-1].kind == "last-exchange":
        return _breakdown(run, story, show, rng)
    if _time_to_listen(run, show, played_s, rng):
        return _repair(run, story, show, rng)
    ended = _aftermath(run)
    if ended:
        return _free(run, story, show, rng, slot="aftermath", words=ended[1], recollects=ended[0])
    if _orientation_due(run, show):
        return _orientation(run, story, show, rng, sign_on=False)
    recalled = _recollection_due(run, show, rng)
    if recalled:
        return _free(run, story, show, rng, slot="recollection", words=recalled[1], recollects=recalled[0])
    return _free(run, story, show, rng)
```

::: {.small-note}
`app/show/director.py` — the whole decision ladder of the show
:::

::: {.notes}
No agent framework: a ladder of ifs. The highlighted line is why the same seed replays the same show — every round
draws from a random generator seeded with the run's seed and the round's number.

WHY A DIRECTOR IN CODE (decision record ADR-0003, 2026-09-21; accepted 2026-09-23 after a gate experiment) —
TalkWithMe made one LLM request per persona, each with its own system prompt, and rewrote the others' lines as
"[Name]: text" user messages. Field-observed problems: labels leaking into speech, a two-role chat template wearing a
four-actor play, random followers, nobody owning the story. The new engine: ONE shared context in screenplay form —
the cast sheet as the system message, then alternating turns: the director's instruction (user) and the script lines
(assistant) — and ONE streamed request per round for the whole exchange. A director in code owns the story; the
model only writes lines. Bonus: llama.cpp's prompt cache reuses only an identical prefix, which per-persona prompts
defeated and one shared context keeps.

WHERE THE DESIGN CAME FROM — the owner's 2024 prototype: the radio "breaks" to cover the listening window; the cast
broadcast among themselves; when it is fixed, they call out and the mic opens about 10 s; a caller makes them pivot
to hope, ask for a name, a location, help to escape, supplies; after some exchanges the radio breaks again. Decoded on
2026-09-26 into two modes, Broadcast and Contact.

THE ROUND KINDS (app/show/director.py, about 800 lines)
- Broadcast, the receiver off: the sign-on (round 1); orientation repeats every 20 ± 5 free rounds, for listeners
  just tuning in; free rounds — 2-3 speakers (whoever has been silent longest first), 1-4 lines weighted toward 2-3,
  holding an event every 2 ± 1 free rounds, the aftermath of a contact, or a recollection of an earlier caller every
  15 ± 5; the call ("repair") between 60 and 180 s of played audio after the receiver went off.
- Contact, the receiver on: an exchange when the listener spoke (the addressed character answers first, 2-3 lines,
  quoting what the voice said, adding one agenda item, ending on a question); a re-call after a silence; the last
  exchange at the 5 ± 1th answer; then the breakdown; two silences in a row and the receiver is switched off.
- The page listens after three kinds: the repair (the call), an exchange, a re-call. ("invitation" in the code is a
  kind from records made before the modes, kept so old runs still load.)

WHAT IT DRAWS FROM — the story's data, not code: lab-outbreak has 289 events, 9 agenda items (the first — who are
you — opens every contact; the rest at random, never twice in a contact), about 500 tone words, and three overtones
with their moods: positive (happy, hopeful, excited, relieved), neutral (calm, doubtful, urgent, curious,
determined), negative (sad, afraid, terrified, angry, exhausted). A free round holds its overtone for 4 ± 1 rounds,
then drifts to a neighbour; a tone word holds 3 ± 1 rounds.

THE SEED — random.Random(f"{run.seed}:{n}"): one generator per round, seeded with the run's seed and the round's
number, so a round's choices do not depend on how many random draws earlier rounds made. With show.seed set, the
same seed gives the same show, word for word, on the same box and build (proven 2026-09-22).
:::

## A grammar keeps the model in format {.grammar-slide}

The grammar the app sent to llama.cpp for one round:

```{.ebnf}
root    ::= line{1,3}
line    ::= speaker " (" emotion "): " text "\n"
speaker ::= "Daniel" | "Moira" | "Ralph"
emotion ::= "sad" | "afraid" | "terrified" | "angry" | "exhausted"
text    ::= [^\n\[\]()]+
```

[What the model wrote under it:]{.wrote-label}

::: {.model-lines}
Daniel (exhausted): We’ve lost power to the security cameras. Over.

Moira (afraid): The samples—they’re spreading. Faster than the math says. Over.

Ralph (angry): This isn’t natural. Someone \*made\* this. Over.
:::

::: {.small-note}
Round 3 of a run on 2026-10-02: only the round's speakers, only the moods allowed, at most three lines
:::

::: {.notes}
GBNF, llama.cpp's grammar format: the model cannot write anything else. A name outside the round, a missing mood, a
fourth line — impossible, not just discouraged. Real request and real output, from the run's debug files.

GBNF = GGML BNF: Backus-Naur Form in the dialect of GGML, the tensor library under llama.cpp. Sent in the request's
top-level "grammar" field; llama.cpp applies it in the sampler on every token, streamed or not.

READING THE GRAMMAR ON THE SLIDE
- root ::= line{1,3} — one to three lines: the round's line budget, a hard bound, not a request.
- speaker — only the round's speakers; a round may also pin one speaker to the first (or last) line.
- emotion — only the moods of the round's overtone (here the negative five).
- text ::= [^\n\[\]()]+ — anything but a line break, a bracket or a parenthesis: no stage directions, no extra
  lines. The app builds a fresh grammar for every round (app/show/grammar.py, 62 lines).

WHY A SCREENPLAY GRAMMAR, NOT JSON (ADR-0003) — the owner's reason: a JSON format confines the model to the
distribution of JSON it saw in training. The quality cost of constrained decoding comes from the model conditioning on
a JSON-looking prefix, not from the mask itself; "Name (mood): words" keeps it inside plain text it knows.

WHAT IT COSTS — MEASURED (experiments of 2026-09-22, the A6000)
- When the grammar agrees with the model: 0.3 % per token (plain "Name: text", the ADR-0003 gate), and 0.5 % with the
  emotion field once the prompt teaches it — and the same text, word for word, with or without the grammar.
- When it must overrule the model: 10.4 % per token (11.27 → 12.44 ms), forcing emotion tags a prompt never asked
  for. In the first round the model even turned its lines into quoted dialogue, conditioning on its own forced tokens;
  from round 2, with plain lines to copy, the quotes disappeared.
- Taught by the prompt, with no grammar at all, 40 of 40 lines carried a legal tag: the grammar is insurance.
- Variety: 8 of the 9 emotions used in every arm, no collapse onto one; taught, the model never once picked "happy" in
  a zombie outbreak.

THE RULE THAT CAME OUT OF IT — every constraint the grammar enforces is also said in the instruction, in the same
words each time ("Moira speaks first, then Daniel or Ralph", "the next three lines", "each with the emotion in its
voice, one of: …"). A grammar that contradicts its prompt changes the model's style and costs more; one that agrees
changes no word. Asked for up to four lines, the model writes four.

READ THE CHAT TEMPLATE FIRST — the grammar constrains only what the model generates, which starts where the template
leaves off. Nemotron's template ends with an empty, closed <think></think> after /no_think, and with an open <think>
without it: a grammar starting with "Name" would then force the script into the model's private reasoning.
:::

## The 32k context, and the trim

```{=html}
{{< include images/_trim_chart.svg >}}
```

::: {.small-note}
A 270-round show, 2026-10-01: rounds cut from the middle (the first 2 and last 4 kept), and the show goes on
:::

::: {.notes}
Budget 34,000 tokens; the trim fires at 90 % (30,600) and cuts down to 50 % (17,000). It landed at 16,608 and 16,722.
A flaw found that day: the trim used to over-cut, more with every trim; fixed and measured — now it lands within one
round of its target.

THE PROBLEM — the show is one growing script: every round the model reads all of it (the cast sheet, every kept
round's instruction and reply, the new instruction). It must fit llama.cpp's context: 16,384 tokens until 2026-10-01,
32,768 since. The trim keeps it inside by removing whole rounds from the middle.

HOW THE APP COUNTS — it does not count tokens itself: it keeps the model server's own count from each round's last
streamed chunk — prompt_n (read fresh), cache_n (reused from the cache), predicted_n (written). Their sum is the
script's size. Example, round 113 of a drive: 203 fresh + 27,653 cached + 50 written = 27,906. Each round records its
share (what it added); the largest seen in 1,824 rounds: 741 tokens (an exchange).

THE TRIM, STEP BY STEP — before each round that asks the model: below 30,600, nothing. At or above it, the rounds
still read become candidates except the first 2 and the last 4; the middle one is cut, then outwards, each taking its
share off, until the estimate reaches 17,000. Cut rounds stay in the record; the model just stops reading them. The
next round's server count is the truth, so an error never adds up.

THE PAUSE AFTER A TRIM — llama.cpp's cache holds only an unbroken start of the prompt; cutting the middle means the
rest is read fresh: about 8.4 s at 32k (13,922 tokens re-read), once every 100 rounds or more. At 16k with a 14,000
budget: every 22-36 rounds, about 5 s each. With 32k: trims 3-4 times rarer, about 60 % longer, and the model keeps
about 2.2 times as much of the show.

WHY 34,000 IF THE CONTEXT IS 32,768 — the trim fires at 90 % of the budget, so the budget may exceed the context as
long as 90 % of it plus room for the next instruction (1,000) and the reply (512) fits: 30,600 + 1,000 + 512 = 32,112
≤ 32,768. When a run opens, the app asks llama.cpp its real context (GET /props) and refuses the run with the
arithmetic if it does not fit (tested with a budget of 40,000: refused). The owner (2026-09-28): "I want to keep as
much context as possible".

THE MEMORY — llama.cpp reserves the context when it starts: going from 16k to 32k cost 206 MiB at once, then 76 MiB on
first use, then nothing more, flat through a full context and a trim (a hybrid model: only 4 attention layers).

THE FLAW, FOUND AND FIXED (2026-10-01, evening) — the round after the first trim had a negative share (−2,837): the
trim had removed more than it estimated. The cause: the call (the Repair) asks the model nothing, so the server reports
no size after it, and two rounds per call had no recorded weight — about 600-850 tokens uncounted per call in the cut
stretch. The error was not constant (the owner's doubt was right): it grew with the calls removed, and compounded,
because a negative share made the next trim cut more. The owner's idea: trigger the trim only in the right round. The
fix: a round after a Repair counts from the last size the server reported, and the trim fires only before a round
that asks the model. Measured with a small budget (8,000) to get many trims: before, the estimate was off by 641 to
4,218 tokens and landed 17-45 % low; after, off by 1 to 3 tokens on every trim, landing within one round of its
target. The owner: "it makes the show forget more lines that we intended" — now it forgets what it intends, and no
more.
:::

## One command to a GPU {.smaller .gpu-slide}

```bash
make ans-deploy ENV=cloud
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Four roles, each for its own machines:

- **base**: checks Ubuntu, Docker, the NVIDIA toolkit and driver (never installs them)
- **llama**: llama.cpp in a pinned container, the model from Hugging Face
- **tts_engine**: tts-serve 1.2 as a system service
- **stt_engine**: Whisper in a container
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.stats .one .compact}
::: {.stat}
[7 minutes]{.n}<br>from a fresh VM to the stack running
:::
::: {.stat}
[changed=0]{.n}<br>a second run changes nothing
:::
::: {.stat}
[~$0.50 an hour]{.n}<br>an RTX A6000, 48 GB, on Hyperstack
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
From zero in 7 minutes (ok=33 changed=16); the re-run reports changed=0 in 30 seconds. Before touching anything, the
playbook checks it is aimed at the right environment and that no placeholder is left. The price: $0.50-0.59 an hour,
from our provider survey of 2026-09-13 — check today's price before the talk.

WHY IT MATTERS — the owner's framing (2026-09-17): "deployment is 50% of the MVP". The deployment machinery was the
arc's deliverable #1, built and proven live on 2026-09-18, before the show engine existed.

THE SHAPE — one playbook (site.yml), four roles, about 475 lines of YAML. It starts at "an SSH-able Ubuntu box exists":
creating the VM stays in the provider's console, so nothing is provider-specific. Inventories per environment (cloud,
local); addresses live in the repo only as a REPLACE_ME placeholder. Roles gate themselves: each applies only on hosts
in its own inventory group. Privilege: root declared once, at the play level; any task that runs as another user says
so explicitly.

HOW EACH SERVICE IS SUPERVISED — llama.cpp and Whisper: detached Docker containers with restart unless-stopped, so
Docker brings them back; tts-serve: a systemd unit, enabled. All three survive SSH disconnects, crashes and reboots
without an operator (after a reboot: back in under a minute). No tmux anywhere — the owner: a hard no.

PINNED, ON PURPOSE — llama.cpp image build b11096; whisper-fastapi pinned by digest; tts-serve tag 1.2; the CUDA
generation (cu128) and torch 2.9.1 as project variables. The base role asserts the driver can run that CUDA
generation — added after a live crash loop on 2026-09-18: a CUDA 13 build on an R570 driver ("driver too old").

REJECTED, AND WHY — docker-compose: a good pattern, but overkill for two containers with short, proven docker run
commands, no traffic between them, one operator and a 3-day timebox (flip trigger: services with dependencies).
Terraform / VM provisioning: out of scope for v1.

WHAT A FRESH BOX TAUGHT US (2026-09-22) — a new Ubuntu VM spends its first hour in its own updater (259 packages, 43
minutes); our deploy hit apt's lock and failed. The fix: a configurable wait for the lock (300 s), announced in the
task's name, and a plain explanation if it times out. Hence "7 minutes once apt has finished".

THE COST — an RTX A6000, 48 GB, at $0.50-0.59 an hour, Hyperstack (the cheapest suitable GPU in the survey, twice the
memory floor). A stopped VM keeps billing; only hibernation stops the meter, with a stock lottery on restore.
:::
